lesson.child_mission: Capacity and volume fluency converts mL↔L and counts cube volumes with clear cubic or millilitre units.
lesson.evidence_instructions: Save the independent response, specific revisions and both short-answer explanations; record oral evidence for speaking tasks.
lesson.extension: Apply the same method to a larger number or a new context, then compare two solution paths for accuracy.
lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Convert 1500 mL; volume 3×3×3; compare 500 mL and 0.5 L.

FEEDBACK
1 L 500 mL; 27 cubic units; equal.

WATCH FOR
Mixing mL with cubic centimetres without context can confuse different measures.

INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Complete a sixteen-item capacity/volume fluency set. Re-work misses with unit labels rewritten.

Write a short reflection naming one step you corrected and why.

lesson.parent_notes:
Parent: Marking guidance for the independent task: Complete a sixteen-item capacity/volume fluency set. Re-work misses with unit labels rewritten. Accept equivalent original responses that show the same skill.

Parent: Written model 1: Original response on new material: 1 L 500 mL; 27 cubic units; equal. Reasoning: I used fluency by attending to capacity and explain why it matters rather than copying the worked model.

Parent: Written model 2: Common error: Mixing mL with cubic centimetres without context can confuse different measures. Correction: 1 L 500 mL; 27 cubic units; equal. Why: the correction restores accurate use of fluency.

Parent: Likely misconception: Mixing mL with cubic centimetres without context can confuse different measures. Keep sample answers out of the child role.

Parent: Short-answer focus 1: Solve one fresh problem that uses fluency with different numbers from the worked model. Show working and name the places or values that matter.

Parent: Short-answer focus 2: Describe one likely mistake with fluency, show corrected working, and say why the correction works.

teach_steps.explain:
Capacity and volume fluency converts mL↔L and counts cube volumes with clear cubic or millilitre units.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner choose methods based on place value, quantity and accurate working, rather than guessing digits by shape alone. Keep every step justified.

HOW TO WORK
Read the worked example and name the places, values or distances that carry the method. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. Compare your working with the feedback: did you use the same skill and show your reasoning? If a digit or place is uncertain, identify what would have to be regrouped or counted again. One deliberate, justified revision is more useful than writing a longer answer.
